### Problem: Top K Frequent Elements {#sec-lts-p3-b}

::: {.p-statement}

Given `nums` ($1 \le n \le 10^5$, $-10^4 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 10^4$) and $k$ ($1 \le k \le$ #distinct), return the $k$ most frequent elements in any order; the answer set is guaranteed unique. The follow-up demands better than $O(n \log n)$.

Source: [LC 347 · Top K Frequent Elements](https://leetcode.com/problems/top-k-frequent-elements/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example — `nums = [1,1,1,2,2,3], k = 2`. Output `[1, 2]` (counts 3 and 2).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Sorting values by frequency is $O(n \log n)$. But frequencies are themselves small integers in $[1, n]$, so invert the buckets: index an array *by count* and store the values having that count. Walking the buckets from $n$ down collects the most common values first — stop after $k$. No comparisons; total $O(n)$. This is @sec-lts-p3-a's idea, cut short.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Count, sort by count.** `Counter.most_common(k)` sorts the distinct values by frequency and slices. $O(n + A \log A)$ — the oracle (and, for $A$ distinct values, only mildly superlinear).
2. **Frequency buckets.** Histogram, then `buckets[count].append(value)`; scan $f = n \downarrow 1$ collecting until $k$ values are gathered. $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.

**Invariant.** A value is stored in exactly the bucket equal to its frequency, so a downward scan visits values in non-increasing frequency; the first $k$ collected are the $k$ most frequent, and the uniqueness guarantee means the cut at $k$ never lands mid-tie.
:::

The buttons are in order: lean on `most_common`, then beat it with the count-as-index trick.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Count and sort

::: {.form-next}
Histogram the values, take the top $k$ of `most_common`. $O(n + A \log A)$, $O(A)$ space; correct and the baseline for the stress test.

**Worked example.** `1:3, 2:2, 3:1`; most_common(2) → `[1, 2]`.
:::

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("topk", "sort")
    assert str(final) == "[1, 2]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def tkf347_sort(nums, k):
    c = Counter(nums)
    return [x for x, _ in c.most_common(k)]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// sort the distinct values by frequency, keep k
vector<int> tkf347Sort(vector<int> nums, int k) {
    unordered_map<int, int> c;
    for (int x : nums) ++c[x];
    vector<int> u;
    for (auto& p : c) u.push_back(p.first);
    sort(u.begin(), u.end(), [&](int a, int b) { return c[a] > c[b]; });
    u.resize(k);
    return u;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `most_common` is a heapq-backed sort-by-count; the C++ sorts the *distinct* values only, so it is $O(A \log A)$ after the $O(n)$ count. Good, but the follow-up wants strictly linear — which the buckets provide because a count needs no sorting.

#### Frequency buckets (linear)

::: {.form-next}
Histogram, drop each value into `buckets[frequency]`, then walk $f = n \downarrow 1$ collecting values until $k$ are taken. $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.

**Worked example.** `bucket[3]=[1], bucket[2]=[2], bucket[1]=[3]`. Read down: `1, 2` — that is $k=2$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("topk", "bucket")
    assert str(final) == "[1, 2]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-347-bucket
def tkf347_bucket(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    c = Counter(nums)
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for x, f in c.items():
        buckets[f].append(x)
    res = []
    for f in range(n, 0, -1):
        for x in buckets[f]:
            res.append(x)
            if len(res) == k:
                return res
    return res

for _ in range(300):
    nums = [random.randint(-6, 6) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 25))]
    uniq = len(set(nums))
    kk = random.randint(1, uniq)
    counts = sorted(Counter(nums).values(), reverse=True)
    if kk < uniq and counts[kk - 1] == counts[kk]:
        continue                                    # the top-k set is not unique: not a valid input
    assert sorted(tkf347_bucket(nums, kk)) == sorted(tkf347_sort(nums, kk))
assert sorted(tkf347_bucket([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 2)) == [1, 2]
assert tkf347_bucket([1], 1) == [1]
assert tkf347_bucket([1, 2], 2) in ([1, 2], [2, 1])
print("tkf347_bucket OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// bucket values by frequency, harvest the top k in O(n)
vector<int> tkf347Bucket(vector<int> nums, int k) {
    unordered_map<int, int> c;
    for (int x : nums) ++c[x];
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    vector<vector<int>> buckets(n + 1);
    for (auto& p : c) buckets[p.second].push_back(p.first);
    vector<int> res;
    for (int f = n; f >= 1 && (int)res.size() < k; --f)
        for (int x : buckets[f]) { res.push_back(x); if ((int)res.size() == k) break; }
    return res;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The `if len(res) == k: return` short-circuit is the difference between @sec-lts-p3-a (emit the *whole* sorted string) and here (stop at $k$): same bucket structure, earlier exit. The stress test compares as *sets* (`sorted(...)`) because the problem accepts any order, and it skips random inputs where the $k$-th and $(k+1)$-th counts tie: the problem promises those never occur, and on them two correct programs may legitimately return different sets.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Count + sort** is $O(n + A \log A)$ time. **Frequency buckets** is $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space. A third route — a size-$k$ min-heap of (count, value) — is $O(n + A \log k)$; see @sec-salgo for the heap view of "keep the best $k$."
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $k$ equals the number of distinct values: the whole value set, in frequency order.
- A value counted once lives in `bucket[1]`; it is only taken if the window reaches count 1.
- Single element `[1], k=1` → `[1]`.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [LC 1481 · Least Number of Unique Integers after K Removals](https://leetcode.com/problems/least-number-of-unique-integers-after-k-removals/){difficulty="Medium"} — the same frequency buckets, scanned from the *smallest* count up.
:::
